replies.raw:
When you hit send, the model never sees your words. It sees numbers.

Your text gets chopped into pieces called **tokens**, which are often whole words but sometimes word fragments or punctuation. Each token is then swapped for a number. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 tokens, and every piece of text you ever send is built from that fixed menu.

[KEY]An LLM doesn't read words; it reads a sequence of numbers that stand in for chunks of text.[/KEY]

[EX]Take the sentence "The cat sat on the mat." A tokenizer might split it into pieces like "The", " cat", " sat", " on", " the", " mat", ".", and then map each piece to a number (say 464, 3797, 3332... these IDs are made up for illustration, since every tokenizer uses different ones).[/EX]

[Q]
Why does a model work with tokens converted to numbers instead of reading raw words?
A) Numbers let the model look up the answer in a database
B) Words are too long for computers to store
C) Neural networks do math, so text must become numbers first
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) Neural networks do math, so text must become numbers first
replies.raw:
Right. A neural network is built from arithmetic, so text has to become numbers before it can do anything with it.

Now the part that surprises most people: once your tokens are in, the model does one job, over and over. It predicts the **next token**.

It doesn't look up an answer anywhere. It reads the tokens so far and produces a probability for every token in its roughly 100,000-token vocabulary, then picks one. That token gets added to the text, and the whole process repeats for the next one.

[EX]Take "The cat sat on the ___". The model might give "mat" a high probability, "floor" and "couch" smaller ones, and "democracy" a tiny one. When one continuation dominates, the model is confident. When many fit, the probability is spread thin.[/EX]

[KEY]An LLM generates text by repeatedly predicting a probability for each possible next token, then picking one.[/KEY]

[Q]
What best describes how an LLM produces an answer to your question?
A) It builds the answer one token at a time from probabilities
B) It writes the full answer at once, then checks it
C) It searches its stored text for the best match
ANS: A
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) It writes the full answer at once, then checks it
replies.raw:
Not quite. That's a common picture, but it isn't how generation works. The model doesn't draft a full answer and then check it.

It produces one token at a time: predict, add that token to the text, then predict again with the new text as input.

Think of your phone's autocomplete, but run in a loop. Each word it writes becomes part of the input for choosing the next one.

[EX]Imagine the prompt "The capital of France is". The model predicts " Paris" and adds it to the text. Now the input is "The capital of France is Paris", and it predicts again, maybe a period. Then it predicts whether to stop or keep going. No complete answer ever existed before the tokens started appearing.[/EX]

[KEY]The answer you see is built token by token, with each new token chosen after the previous ones are already written.[/KEY]

Let's try it again from a fresh angle.

[Q]
Right after the model picks one token, what happens next?
A) It stops and waits for you to approve the token
B) It rereads the whole question from scratch and discards that token
C) It adds the token to the text and predicts the next one
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) It adds the token to the text and predicts the next one
replies.raw:
Yes, that's the loop. Predict, add the token, predict again, until the model decides to stop.

There's one more idea to cover before you try it yourself. Look at the word "bank" in these two sentences:

- "I sat on the bank of the river."
- "I put cash in the bank."

The tokenizer gives "bank" the same token both times. So how does the model know which meaning is in play?

It uses a mechanism called **attention**. As the model processes each token, it weighs how much to focus on every other token around it. In the first sentence, "bank" attends strongly to "river."

In the second, it attends to "cash."

[EX]Compare "I went to the bank" with the two sentences above. On its own, that one is genuinely ambiguous, because nothing in "went," "to," or "the" settles the meaning. Attention can only use the context that's actually there.[/EX]

[KEY]Attention lets the model use the surrounding tokens to work out what a word means in this particular sentence.[/KEY]

[Q]
In "I put cash in the bank," what lets the model treat "bank" as a financial place?
A) The word "bank" has a different token ID in this sentence
B) Attention to nearby words like "cash" shapes its meaning
C) The model looks "bank" up in a dictionary of definitions
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) Attention to nearby words like "cash" shapes its meaning
replies.raw:
Correct. The token for "bank" is identical in both sentences, and it's attention to the surrounding words, like "cash" or "river," that settles the meaning.

Now let's put this to work. Here are three sentences, each ending in a blank where the model must predict the next token:

1. "The cat sat on the ___."
2. "After dinner, we decided to go ___."
3. "The capital of France is ___."

[Q]
Why is the model more confident filling in "The cat sat on the ___" than "My favorite thing about summer is ___"?
A) One continuation is far more probable than the others
B) The second sentence contains words the model can't tokenize
C) The model remembers seeing that exact sentence in training
D) The first sentence is shorter, so it takes less processing
ANS: A
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) The second sentence contains words the model can't tokenize
replies.raw:
Not quite. Tokenizers can break any text into tokens, so the second sentence tokenizes just fine. Confidence has nothing to do with whether the words can be tokenized.

Let me come at it from another angle. Imagine the model has to guess your next word in two situations.

If you say "Happy birthday to ___", almost everyone says "you". One answer wins by a mile.

If you say "For dinner tonight I want ___", pizza, pasta, tacos, soup and a hundred other answers all work. The model's probability gets split across many options, so no single token stands out.

So confidence depends on how many plausible continuations exist and how lopsided they are.

[KEY]The model's confidence is high when one next token dominates and low when many tokens are plausible.[/KEY]

[Q]
Which sentence would the model fill in with the HIGHEST confidence in its top token?
A) "A good name for my new puppy is ___"
B) "Yesterday I felt really ___"
C) "Roses are red, violets are ___"
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.raw:
Yes, "blue" dominates that poem so heavily that the model is very confident in its top token. A puppy name or a feeling could be filled in a hundred ways, so the probability gets spread thin.

You've now seen both halves: text becomes tokens, then the model predicts one token at a time.

2. "After the movie, we decided to get ___"

Here's something that surprises most people: the model never sees your words. It sees numbers.

Before anything else happens, your prompt gets chopped into chunks called **tokens**, and each chunk is swapped for a number. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of these chunks.

[KEY]An LLM doesn't read words, it reads tokens: chunks of text turned into numbers.[/KEY]

[EX]Imagine the sentence "I put cash in the bank." The tokenizer might split it into pieces like "I", " put", " cash", " in", " the", " bank", "." and give each piece an ID number (made-up numbers here, just for illustration: 40, 3009, 8515, 304, 279, 6201, 13).[/EX]

Notice that "bank" gets the same token whether it means money or a riverbank. The model sorts that out later, from the words around it.

[Q]
What does an LLM actually receive when you type a prompt?
A) Search terms it looks up in a database of stored answers
B) Your text chopped into chunks, each turned into a number
C) Your sentence as a whole, with its meaning already understood
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked B) Your text chopped into chunks, each turned into a number
replies.raw:
Yes, that's it. And notice what's missing: the model isn't looking anything up. It's working with numbers from the start.

Now for what it does with those numbers. The model's one core job is to predict the **next token**, over and over.

Given everything so far, it scores every token in its vocabulary by how likely it is to come next. Then it picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats.

[KEY]An LLM writes by repeatedly predicting the most plausible next token, one at a time.[/KEY]

[EX]Take "The cat sat on the ___". The model would put a very high score on "mat" or "floor" and almost none on "democracy". But "My favorite food is ___" has hundreds of reasonable endings, so the model's scores are spread thin across many tokens.[/EX]

That difference matters: sometimes one continuation dominates, and sometimes the field is wide open.

[Q]
Why is "The cat sat on the ___" easier for a model to predict than "My favorite food is ___"?
A) The sentence is shorter, so there are fewer tokens to process
B) One or two continuations fit far better than all the others
C) The model has stored this exact sentence and recalls its ending
ANS: B
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) The model has stored this exact sentence and recalls its ending
replies.raw:
Not quite, and that's a very common mix-up. It's the same "looking things up" idea from earlier, showing up in a new costume.

The model doesn't store sentences and recall their endings. During training it absorbed patterns about which words tend to follow which, so it never needs to have seen this exact sentence. A brand-new sentence like "The purple walrus sat on the ___" still gets sensible predictions, because the pattern (something sat on something) is what carries the weight.

So why is the cat sentence easier? Because after "sat on the", only a few endings fit well, like "mat" or "floor", and they soak up nearly all the probability. With "My favorite food is ___", hundreds of endings fit, so the probability is spread thin.

[KEY]Confidence comes from how many continuations fit, not from remembering a stored sentence.[/KEY]

Let's check that with a fresh example.

[Q]
Which blank would a model predict with the MOST confidence?
A) "On weekends I like to ___"
B) "I'm in the mood for ___"
C) "Thank you so much, I really ___"
ANS: C
[/Q]

replies.user: I picked C) "Thank you so much, I really ___"
replies.raw:
Right, "Thank you so much, I really ___" has a clear favorite. "Appreciate it" soaks up most of the probability, while the other two blanks could end a hundred different ways. That's the same idea as the cat sentence: confidence comes from how many continuations fit.

One more idea to round this out. Take another look at "bank" from earlier. It gets the same token whether it means money or a river, so how does the model tell which one you mean?

It uses a mechanism called **attention**. As the model processes each token, it weighs how much to "look at" every other token in the text. The surrounding words push the meaning in one direction or the other.

[KEY]Attention lets each token be interpreted in light of the other tokens around it.[/KEY]

[EX]In "I sat on the bank of the river", attention ties "bank" strongly to "river", pushing the prediction toward water and mud. In "I put cash in the bank", it ties "bank" to "cash", pushing toward money.[/EX]
